characters: Benewaa: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform and a sun hat, with a sketchbook.
Dakurah: a 13-year-old boy in a school uniform, with a camera and a water bottle.
Madam Asamoah: their teacher, in a green dress, carrying a clipboard and a seedling.
The river: a wide river seen in two imagined futures, one brown and empty, one clear with trees and fish (story picture).
music: A slow, sad tune for the dry future, brightening into a flowing, hopeful melody for the clear river (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The pupils and teacher are invented. The two futures are imagined by the characters and are not predictions.
The Rhine and Singapore River are used as examples that rivers can recover, not as models to copy exactly.
Every role in the story has a promise, so that no group is made the only villain or the only hero.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: recovery estimate of 10 to 20 years (a Daily Graphic editorial); the Rhine described as biologically dead in the 1970s and now supporting life (the same editorial; confirm with a river-science source); Singapore River cleaned in ten years (NLB Singapore).
Check that each promise is realistic and lawful and that none names a real person.
Check that the story does not suggest that children alone can fix the problem.

teacherGuide.overview: A closing story that imagines two futures for a river and asks every role to make a promise. It teaches that change needs a shared effort, that promises must be specific, and that children can lead by example.
learningGoals: Describe two possible futures for a river and what makes each one happen.
Write specific promises for different roles.
Make and share a personal promise.
beforeReading: Ask: if you could see your river in twenty years, what would you hope to see?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners to write one promise for a leader and one for themselves.
afterReading: Make a “promise wall” in class and revisit it each term.
Plant a tree and photograph it each year.
discussion: Why are specific promises better than slogans?
How can we keep each other to our promises?
reflection: What is one promise you will keep this month?

mathsExtension.task: Benewaa is 13. How old will she be in 20 years?
A class plants one tree each year for 20 years. How many trees is that?

stretch: Choose a local river or stream and write a ten-year restoration plan.

culturalNotes: The pupils and teacher are invented. The two futures are imagined by the characters and are not predictions.
The Rhine and Singapore River are used as examples that rivers can recover, not as models to copy exactly.
Every role in the story has a promise, so that no group is made the only villain or the only hero.
localiseThis: Use your own river and local leaders; invite a leader to read the promises and respond.

whatWeKnow: Rivers can recover when people decide to heal them, but it takes years.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: How long it will take Ghana’s rivers, and which actions matter most.

factCheck.claim: Recovery may take 10 to 20 years of consistent work (an estimate); the Rhine was declared biologically dead in the 1970s and now supports life after investment and enforcement; recommended a Water Restoration Fund, river-by-river restoration plans, monthly public data and enforcement against financiers.
factCheck.explanation: From a Daily Graphic editorial, which is opinion; the Rhine claim should be confirmed with a river-science source.
factCheck.reference: Graphic Online, “Can Ghana heal her water?” (12 August 2026).

factCheck.claim: The Singapore River clean-up took about ten years (1977 to 1987).
factCheck.explanation: From the National Library Board Singapore’s encyclopedia entry.
factCheck.reference: NLB Singapore, Infopedia, “Cleaning of the Singapore River”.

narrationPlan.voice: Reflective voices for Benewaa and Dakurah; warm, steady voice for Madam Asamoah
narrationPlan.pace: Reflective and hopeful, slower at the two futures (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.
